items.explain: Projecting the path-space problem onto its endpoints gives entropic OT between the two marginals. Diffusion Schrödinger bridges solve it iteratively with score-based models.

items.prompt: What is a diffusion transformer (DiT)?
choices: Latent diffusion with a transformer denoiser over patch tokens, replacing the U-Net
A generative transformer that drops the diffusion objective entirely
A U-Net denoiser with one attention layer added at its bottleneck
A transformer language model trained with a diffusion-style loss on text
items.explain: DiT conditions transformer blocks on timestep and class. Peebles and Xie report that sample quality improves with transformer compute.

items.prompt: If you swap a diffusion model's U-Net for a transformer, what must change?
choices: The noise must become non-Gaussian
Only the denoiser architecture
Sampling becomes one forward pass
It is no longer a diffusion model
items.explain: Backbone and generative objective are separate design axes, so the diffusion training objective and sampler can stay the same. That is why DiT can reuse standard diffusion training.

items.prompt: What does SINDy (sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics) do?
choices: Computes the Fourier spectrum of the measured trajectory
Trains a deep black-box network to predict the next state
Sparse regression of derivatives onto a library of candidate terms
Fits one linear model that keeps every library term active
items.explain: Sparsity keeps the identified ODE short and readable. SINDYc adds control inputs to the library.

items.prompt: Why do SINDy results depend on the chosen coordinates and library?
choices: The library only affects computation time, never the identified model
They do not: sparse regression is coordinate-free, so any coordinates work
With noise-free data SINDy always finds the true law, whatever the library
The dynamics are sparse only if few library terms in those coordinates suffice
items.explain: Sparsity is a property of a representation, not of the system alone. A poor library or coordinate choice can need many terms or fail to represent the dynamics.

items.prompt: What is the Koopman operator of a dynamical system x ↦ F(x)?
choices: The Jacobian of F at a fixed point
The linear operator on observables, Kg = g ∘ F
The Hessian of the system's energy
A nonlinear operator acting on the state
items.explain: The Koopman operator is generally infinite-dimensional; it trades nonlinear state dynamics for linear dynamics on functions of the state. Learned embeddings seek a few observables that evolve almost linearly.

items.prompt: A Koopman autoencoder learns k observables that evolve linearly. When is this finite linear model exact?
choices: Always, since the Koopman operator is itself linear
Whenever loss on the training trajectories reaches zero
Whenever k exceeds the dimension of the state
Only if the observables span a Koopman-invariant subspace
items.explain: Linearity of the infinite-dimensional operator does not guarantee exact finite closure; Brunton et al. (2016) argue, for example, that a system with several isolated fixed points has no finite-dimensional Koopman-invariant subspace that includes the state with continuous observables. Closure error should be measured before relying on the model.

items.prompt: A Hamiltonian neural network learns a scalar energy H(q, p). How are the dynamics obtained?
choices: q̇ = p, ṗ = −H
items.explain: Deriving dynamics from Hamilton's equations builds conservation of H into the vector field. Flipping the signs gives time-reversed dynamics.

items.prompt: A trained Hamiltonian network integrated with a standard RK4 solver slowly drifts in energy. Why?
choices: Finite steps of a non-symplectic integrator add drift, though the vector field conserves H
Hamiltonian networks cannot conserve energy, even in exact continuous time
Energy drift shows the learned H depends explicitly on time
RK4 is exact for Hamiltonian systems, so the learned network must be wrong
items.explain: Conservation belongs to the exact flow, and discretization is a separate source of error. Symplectic integrators keep energy error bounded over long times.

items.prompt: How is a physics-informed neural network (PINN) trained?
choices: By penalizing the PDE residual at collocation points plus boundary terms
By hard-coding the solution's Fourier coefficients in advance
By learning a map from PDE coefficients to solutions across a family
By running a classical solver and copying only its outputs
items.explain: Physical laws enter the loss as soft constraints, along with initial, boundary and data terms. Learning maps across a PDE family is operator learning, a different construction.

items.prompt: What failure mode does the cited work (Krishnapriyan et al., 2021) document for PINNs?
choices: PINNs cannot represent smooth solutions with standard activations
PINNs always overfit the boundary conditions and ignore all data terms
Adding the physics residual always makes training strictly easier
The soft residual loss can make optimization fail even when the network could fit
items.explain: Residual terms can create hard, ill-conditioned loss landscapes, especially for difficult coefficients. The paper proposes curriculum and sequence-to-sequence training as mitigations.

items.prompt: What does neural operator learning (FNO, DeepONet) aim to learn?
choices: One PDE instance's solution, by minimizing its residual
The Fourier spectrum of one particular signal
A map between function spaces across a family of problems
A classifier for images of differential equations
items.explain: An operator, such as initial condition or coefficients to solution, applies to new inputs in the family without retraining. Online speed must be weighed against the offline training cost.

items.prompt: What does a Fourier neural operator (FNO) layer do?
choices: Attention over grid points in place of any Fourier transform
Learned weights on truncated low-frequency Fourier modes, plus a pointwise linear term
Fixed Fourier filters with no learned parameters, followed by a nonlinearity
Learned weights on every frequency, with the spatial representation discarded
items.explain: The layer FFTs its input, multiplies kept modes by learned weights, inverse-transforms, adds a pointwise linear map and applies a nonlinearity. Truncating modes keeps the parameter count independent of grid resolution.

items.prompt: What does balanced POD use to approximate balanced truncation?
choices: Direct simulation snapshots only, as in standard POD
Direct and adjoint simulation snapshots, combined by an SVD
Random projections of the system's state matrix
Exact dense Gramians from solving Lyapunov equations
items.explain: Adjoint snapshots supply observability information that direct snapshots lack. The SVD of their cross product yields biorthogonal bases and approximate Hankel singular values.

items.prompt: Why use balanced POD instead of exact balanced truncation for a fluid model with 10⁶ states?
choices: Exact balancing needs dense n×n Gramians, infeasible at this size
Exact balanced truncation does not apply to stable linear systems
Balanced POD keeps every state, so it is always more accurate
Lyapunov equations have no solution for systems this large
items.explain: Solving Lyapunov equations for dense 10⁶×10⁶ Gramians is impractical. Balanced POD builds low-rank factors from snapshots, at the cost of approximation in the balancing.

items.prompt: What is GraphCast, the atlas's example of a learned physical forecaster?
choices: A data-assimilation method that estimates the current atmospheric state
A numerical weather model that integrates the primitive equations directly
A graph neural network trained on reanalysis data that rolls out weather forecasts
A diffusion model that generates realistic satellite images of clouds
items.explain: GraphCast learns medium-range, multi-step forecasts from historical reanalysis states. It still needs an analysis of the current state as its starting point.

items.prompt: A deterministic learned forecaster beats a physics model on RMSE. What is needed to evaluate its forecast uncertainty?
choices: Nothing more: a lower RMSE already implies well-calibrated uncertainty
The spread of the deterministic forecast's values across grid points
A longer RMSE evaluation period covering more seasons and regions
A probabilistic or ensemble forecast, scored with proper scores such as CRPS
items.explain: A single deterministic forecast has no predictive distribution to evaluate. Point accuracy and distributional quality are different properties, and proper scores plus coverage checks assess the latter.

items.prompt: What does the Mori–Zwanzig formalism say about projecting dynamics onto resolved variables?
choices: The unresolved variables can be dropped with no effect
They become a linear system with no memory at all
They are always Markovian in the resolved variables alone
They gain a memory term over past history plus unresolved forcing
items.explain: The reduced equations split into an instantaneous term, a memory integral and an orthogonal forcing term. Discarding variables does not discard their influence.

items.prompt: What does Mori–Zwanzig imply when you learn a reduced model from data?
choices: Reduced models should always use only the current resolved state
Memory terms matter only for linear systems, never nonlinear ones
A memoryless reduced model can be insufficient; history can help
Any reduced model becomes exact if it is trained for long enough
items.explain: The memory integral is why delay embeddings or recurrent closures are tested against Markov baselines, for example in learned turbulence models.
